clue.text: Horses carrying little piggies to market?

definitions.meaning: harness-racing horses that trot rather than gallop
pigs' feet, which carry the 'little piggies' of the nursery rhyme to market

explanation.surface: Racehorses are pictured giving piglets a ride to market.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme 'This little piggy went to market' is counted on toes; a pig's feet are its trotters, and they carry it to market.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a horse bred for trotting races and a pig's foot, the part that walks the animal to market.

clue.text: Trifling story about island race

definitions.note: taken as a noun, trifling talk or idle chatter

indicators.note: the word for a story goes about, that is around, the race

parts.note: a story is a tale
the TT is the motorcycle race held on the Isle of Man

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses a tale about a race held on an island as trivial.
explanation.walkthrough: The TT (Tourist Trophy) is the famous motorcycle race on the Isle of Man. 'Trifling' is used as the noun, idle talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Gossip or idle chatter is trifling talk, which is what this word means as a noun.

clue.text: Does a steward initially mull an old red port?

definitions.note: a Black Sea port of the former Soviet Union, red meaning communist

indicators.note: to mull is to stir and heat, so the letters before it are mixed up
only the opening letter of steward is used

explanation.surface: A steward wonders whether to mull a glass of old red port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mull' looks like warming wine, but it stirs DOES + A + S (the first letter of 'steward', signalled by 'initially') into a new order. 'red' means Soviet: the city was a Soviet port.
explanation.definitionFit: This Black Sea harbour city was a major port of the Soviet Union, the 'red' state.

clue.text: Good for a loan? Rather too expensive!

definitions.text: Good for a loan? Rather too expensive!

parts.words: Good for a loan? Rather too expensive!
parts.note: someone easily 'touched' for money is good for a loan, but being asked rankles, so the person is sensitive about it

explanation.surface: A borrower is told a loan would come at too high a price.
explanation.walkthrough: To touch someone is slang for cadging money from them; the clue plays on a person who can be touched and who bristles at the cost.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means easily offended or sensitive, here pictured as someone pestered for loans.

clue.text: Some refuse to be dropped into this place Crete rebuilt

definitions.text: Some refuse to be dropped into this

indicators.note: built again in another form, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Rubbish is to be dumped in a reconstructed site on Crete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rebuilt' rearranges PLACE + CRETE. 'refuse' is the noun rubbish, not the verb to decline.
explanation.definitionFit: A bin is a container into which rubbish is dropped, the general word for any holder.

clue.text: An old fellow very loudly getting into tearing rage

indicators.note: the musical sign is placed inside the rearranged word
a tearing rage is wild, so the word rage is scrambled

parts.note: FF, fortissimo, is the musical marking for very loud

explanation.surface: An elderly man shouts in a furious temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tearing' rearranges the word rage, and 'getting into' puts the musical very-loud mark inside. A gaffer is an old countryman in British use.
explanation.definitionFit: A colloquial British term for an elderly countryman, also used for a boss or foreman.

clue.text: They are said to lead to Rome or Dallas somehow

definitions.text: They are said to lead to Rome

indicators.note: done in some unspecified way, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: Roads to Rome or to Dallas are being compared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges OR + DALLAS. The proverb says every route leads to Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says that every road leads to Rome, so all routes are the ones said to do so.

clue.text: Miss Blondie Scott imagined to be in Perth

definitions.text: Scott imagined to be in Perth

parts.note: a blonde person is fair-haired
a miss is an unmarried girl, a maid

explanation.surface: A fair-haired girl in a Scottish novel lives in Perth.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Walter Scott's novel is The Fair Maid of Perth; the heroine he imagined lives in that Scottish town.
explanation.definitionFit: Scott's fictional heroine Catharine Glover is titled the beautiful girl of Perth in his novel.

clue.text: Took umbrage at being dispatched into the wet vegetation

indicators.note: the dispatched word goes inside the plant word

parts.note: a reed is a plant of marshes and wet ground
something dispatched has been sent

explanation.surface: Someone sent out into soggy undergrowth was offended.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being dispatched' looks like part of a picture of someone sent out, but it simply supplies a synonym; 'into' signals the insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: To take umbrage at something is to feel aggrieved or bitter about it.

clue.text: Those nimble bodies who have not yet lost their spirit

definitions.meaning: people who are fast and lively on their feet

definitions.text: bodies who have not yet lost their spirit
definitions.meaning: the living, as in the phrase '... and the dead'

explanation.surface: Agile people who still keep up their morale are praised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quick' once meant alive, as in the Creed's 'the quick and the dead'; spirit is the soul that leaves a body at death.
explanation.definitionFit: Quick means both nimble and, in old usage, living, so the phrase covers agile people and the not-yet-dead.

clue.text: Joins everything that is before September first

indicators.note: the earlier pieces come before the initial

parts.note: everything is all
i.e. abbreviates id est, that is

indicators.note: only the opening letter of September is used

explanation.surface: Everything happens before the start of September.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' takes only the initial of September, and 'before' places the other two pieces ahead of it.
explanation.definitionFit: To ally with someone is to join with them in a common cause.

clue.text: Final expectation of a brew of late hops

indicators.note: brewing mixes ingredients, so the letters are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: A brewer hopes for a good result from late-harvested hops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brew' rearranges LATE + HOPS.
explanation.definitionFit: A final hope is the one remaining thing to rely on, a final expectation.

clue.text: He drives milk producers company to article little William first

indicators.note: the short William goes ahead of the article

parts.note: Wm is the short written form of William
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A firm's article about young William comes first.
explanation.walkthrough: Wm is the old written abbreviation of William; 'first' puts WM before AN.
explanation.definitionFit: A herdsman who looks after and herds dairy cattle drives the animals that give milk.

clue.text: Seaman upset the very first native

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor, and 'upset' read as 'up set' places him at the top of a down entry
the very first is the original one

explanation.surface: A sailor knocks over the original inhabitant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' does not mean overturned: read as 'up set', it puts the sailor at the top of this down entry, above the word for the very first.
explanation.definitionFit: An indigenous inhabitant of a land, present from the earliest times, is a native.

clue.text: Pointed telegram warning us to keep out?

parts.note: barbed means having sharp points
a wire is a telegram

explanation.surface: A sharply worded telegram tells us to stay away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pointed' and 'telegram' look like a cutting message, but they are separate words joined.
explanation.definitionFit: Spiked fencing on a perimeter tells intruders to stay off the property.

clue.text: Flag? That's normal!

definitions.meaning: a banner or ensign carried on a pole

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs that flying a flag is nothing unusual.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a banner and the usual or regular level of things.

clue.text: Breaking up is super!

explanation.surface: Someone cheerfully calls a break-up wonderful.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both shattering into bits and, in British slang, excellent or terrific.

clue.text: Sincere Latin

parts.note: a Latin phrase, meaning in good faith, used for something genuine

explanation.surface: Latin is described as an honest language.
explanation.definitionFit: A Latin tag meaning in good faith, now used in English for genuine or sincere.

clue.text: Silly nonsense of a volume about fruit dessert on railway

indicators.note: in an across entry the book and pudding come before the railway, sitting on it
the book word goes about, that is around, the pudding

parts.note: a tome is a large book or volume
a fool is a pudding of puréed fruit and cream

explanation.surface: A book about a fruit pudding served on a train is silly.
explanation.walkthrough: A fool is a British pudding of puréed fruit folded into cream. 'about' signals the container and 'on' sets the result ahead of the railway abbreviation in this across entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Foolish behaviour or horseplay is silly nonsense.

clue.text: Tell if returned meat is tender

indicators.note: the two words are sent back, so read them backwards

explanation.surface: A diner asks to be told whether sent-back meat is tender.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' reads TELL IF backwards. The definition describes a boneless, tender cut of meat.
explanation.definitionFit: A boneless cut such as the undercut of sirloin, prized because the meat is tender.

clue.text: A garden conurbation sounding nicely established

indicators.note: the phrase is said aloud and the place name heard

parts.note: well in means nicely settled or established

explanation.surface: A garden town sounds pleasantly settled.
explanation.walkthrough: Welwyn Garden City is a planned English town in Hertfordshire; said aloud its first word sounds like WELL IN, meaning well established.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the first part of the name of Welwyn Garden City, a planned town in England.

clue.text: If you go this way you won't get right there

definitions.text: If you go this way you won't get right there

parts.words: If you go this way you won't get right there
parts.note: going off the correct route means never arriving properly

explanation.surface: Directions warn that a certain route will not reach the destination.
explanation.definitionFit: To go off course is to wander from the right path and miss the destination.

clue.text: Capital West Indian attraction as a sun resort

indicators.note: read as re-sort, sorting the letters again

explanation.surface: A Caribbean capital is advertised as a sunny holiday resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resort' looks like a holiday spot but means re-sort: rearrange AS A SUN.
explanation.definitionFit: The capital of the Bahamas is a Caribbean tourist destination.

clue.text: Something not at all becoming when middle-age rows divide us

indicators.note: the inner pieces split the pair of letters apart
the centre letter of age is used

parts.note: lines are rows

explanation.surface: Arguments in middle age drive a couple apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'middle-age' gives G, the centre of AGE; 'rows' is LINES, not quarrels; 'divide' puts G + LINES between U and S.
explanation.definitionFit: Unattractiveness is not at all becoming, becoming meaning flattering.

clue.text: A lady boxer joining Uncle Sam's spy network

parts.note: Muhammad Ali was the famous heavyweight boxer
the CIA is the US intelligence agency

explanation.surface: A woman boxer signs up with American intelligence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'joining' sets ALI beside CIA.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a woman's given name, so it names a lady.

clue.text: Blooming tide rising?

definitions.meaning: a rising tide is an ..., something that flows in

explanation.surface: Flowers bloom as the tide comes in.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the phrase as one word: a rising tide is one that flows in.
explanation.definitionFit: Plants with open blossoms are flowering, and an incoming tide is something that flows inward.

clue.text: Tracked Easter offering returned in unusually odd circumstances

indicators.note: read as 'circum-stances', standing around, so the scrambled letters go around the egg
odd letters arranged unusually are rearranged
the gift word is sent back, read backwards

parts.note: an egg is the traditional Easter gift

explanation.surface: An Easter egg is sent back in strange circumstances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusually' rearranges ODD to DOD and 'returned' reverses the Easter gift to GGE; 'circumstances' is split as circum- (around) + stances, so the first goes around the second.
explanation.definitionFit: To dog someone is to follow them closely, so to have tracked them.

clue.text: Where there's no attempt to hide the vulgarity

definitions.text: Where there's no attempt to hide the vulgarity

parts.words: Where there's no attempt to hide the vulgarity
parts.note: coarseness shown openly and shamelessly

explanation.surface: Coarse behaviour is put on open display.
explanation.definitionFit: Flagrant, conspicuous coarseness is shown without any concealment.
